opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that book by Frans de Waal really stuck with me. I think the biggest shift for me was realizing how much of what we call "human uniqueness" is actually an artifact of how we test for intelligence. De Waal makes this point again and again: we design experiments that are basically human-shaped, and then when an animal fails, we conclude the animal isn't smart. But often the test just doesn't match the animal's body, its senses, or the world it lives in. A squirrel's memory for caching food, a bat's echolocation, an octopus solving problems with arms that each have a kind of semi-independent nervous system. These are forms of intelligence that evolved for very different niches.

So it made me much more humble about the idea that there's a single ladder of intelligence with humans sitting at the top. It's more like a bush, with many branches, each species highly adapted in its own way. Humans are special, of course: language, cumulative culture, abstract symbolic reasoning. But I started to see those as one particular solution, not the definition of intelligence itself.

And honestly, that connects very directly to how I think about AI. Right now a lot of the field measures intelligence through language, through benchmarks that look like exams we'd give to people. That's useful, but it carries the same bias de Waal is warning about. Much of what animals do, and much of what we do too, is grounded in perception, in a physical body, in interacting with a 3D world over time. A cat can't write an essay, but its understanding of space, motion, and physics is extraordinary, and our models still struggle with things like that.

So the book pushed me toward the view that if we want to build truly intelligent systems, we shouldn't only chase what makes humans look unique. We should also understand the shared foundations, the visual and spatial and embodied intelligence that so many animals have. Those may be the more fundamental layers, and language sits on top of them rather than replacing them.

r001.rationale: The response describes different forms of intelligence as having evolved in different niches and emphasizes shared foundations across species, presenting intelligence as diverse and evolutionarily connected rather than uniquely human.

fable-5.1.text:
That book really shook something loose for me. Frans de Waal's basic argument is that for a long time, when we tested animals and they "failed," the problem wasn't the animal, it was the test. We kept designing experiments around what humans are good at, and then concluding that animals couldn't do it. Give a chimpanzee a task built around hands and visual puzzles, it does fine. Give an elephant the same task, it fails, and we say elephants aren't that smart. But elephants live through their trunk and their sense of smell. Design the test around the trunk and suddenly the elephant looks brilliant.

What struck me as a researcher is how much that mirrors what we do with models. We build a benchmark, the model does poorly, and we say "it can't reason." Then someone changes the prompt format or the input modality and the capability was there all along. De Waal has this word, umwelt, the perceptual world an organism actually inhabits. Every species has its own, and ours is just one of them. We tend to put human intelligence at the top of a ladder, and everything else somewhere below. He argues it's not a ladder, it's more like a bush. Octopuses, crows, bats, dolphins, each one is intelligent in the way its body and environment demanded.

So the shift for me was from "how close is this thing to a human" to "what is this thing actually good at, and are we even asking the right question." Human uniqueness got a lot less interesting to me as a concept. Language is remarkable, sure, but a bat's echolocation is also remarkable, and we'd never say a bat is "almost human." I think that same humility applies when we look at vision models or multimodal systems. They're not little humans. They have their own umwelt, shaped by their data and their architecture. The honest scientific posture is to try to understand that world on its own terms, rather than keep grading it against ours and feeling either threatened or superior.

r001.rationale: The response describes intelligence as varied across species and rejects a simple ladder, but it does not present intelligence as evolutionarily continuous.

astra-6.text:
It made me more cautious about assuming that humans are the measure of intelligence. We tend to design a task around what we’re good at, give it to another animal, and then interpret failure as a lack of intelligence. But maybe the task doesn’t make sense in that animal’s world. Maybe we’re not asking the right question.

So for me, the shift was from “How close are animals to us?” to “What does intelligence look like for them?” That doesn’t mean humans aren’t distinctive. It means that being distinctive is different from sitting at the top of a single ladder. And that’s a useful perspective when thinking about AI, too: human-like behavior is one lens on intelligence, but it may not capture everything we ought to understand.

r001.rationale: The response rejects a single hierarchy and recognizes varied forms of intelligence, but it does not present intelligence as evolutionarily continuous across species.

sol-6.1.text:
It made me more cautious about assuming that humans are the standard against which every kind of intelligence should be measured. If we design a test around what comes naturally to us, and an animal performs poorly, does that tell us about the animal’s intelligence—or about our ability to ask the right question?

I think the interesting shift is from ranking intelligence on a single scale to appreciating that different forms of intelligence emerge under different constraints. That doesn’t mean humans aren’t distinctive. But it makes human uniqueness something to investigate, rather than something we should assume from the beginning.
